newsitem.title: USA: Tertiary recovery slows Permian production decline.
newsitem.headline: Tertiary recovery slows Permian production decline.

text.p: Increased use of carbon dioxide flooding is slowing the decline in production from mature Permian Basin oil fields in Texas and New Mexico, industry executives and researchers said.

The tertiary recovery technology will add 140,000 barrels per day (bpd) of production in the historic basin this year and an estimated 170,000 bpd by 2002, said Steve Melzer, director of the Petroleum Industry Alliance at the University of Texas Permian Basin in Odessa, Texas.

Carbon dioxide flooding, along with horizontal drilling and three-dimensional seismic technology, have rekindled exploration and production in the Permian, a basin stretching from north central Texas westward into New Mexico that accounts for 15 percent of total domestic oil production.

"I just see a different era of the oil industry that has emerged since the crash in 1986," Melzer said. "Technology has brought back the differential between the costs of producing fields and the price you get for your production."

Oil production in the Permian peaked at about 1.95 million bpd in the early 1970s, and since has been declining steadily. Production this year is running at about 900,000 bpd per day and is expected to fall to 720,000 bpd in 2002, he said.

But the rate of decline has slowed as major oil companies, led by Shell Continental Cos, a Shell Oil Co affilate, found ways to cut costs of carbon dioxide injection and made the technology available to independent producers.
Along with six majors, 11 independents in the Permian use carbon dioxide flooding, including Wiser Oil Co and Mitchell Energy & Development Corp, Melzer said.
Cross Timbers Oil Co this year is developing a carbon dioxide flood plan for its Prentice Northeast unit on the prolific northwest shelf of the basin, the company's largest oil property.

Shell is cultivating a growing market among independents turning to carbon dioxide injection as oil production falls off following natural pressure drops and secondary waterfloods, said Chuck Fox, chief engineer on Shell's carbon dioxide operations.
"Marketing efforts over the past year have resulted in the signing of contracts for over one-half trillion cubic feet of carbon dioxide," he said.

Shell operates the McElmo Dome carbon dioxide field in southwestern Colorado, where production rose from about 550 million cubic feet per day (mmcfd) in the first half of 1995 to more than 800 mmcfd today, and is expected to rise to about 1.1 billion cubic feet per day by late 1998, he said.

About 25 percent of Shell's production from the McElmo Dome and Bravo Dome source field in northeastern New Mexico are committed to Altura Energy Ltd., the Shell-Amoco Co joint venture in the Permian, Fox said.
